rationale: Healthy vegetation strongly reflects near infrared and absorbs red light. NDVI uses this contrast to indicate how much green vegetation each pixel contains (values from -1 to 1).
caveats: Use surface reflectance (atmospherically corrected imagery, level L2A/L2) | Mask clouds and shadows first | In dense forests, such as the Amazon, NDVI saturates: it stays close to 1 and stops discriminating; consider EVI

rationale: Similar to NDVI, but also uses the blue band to reduce atmospheric and soil effects. It saturates less in dense vegetation, which makes it popular in tropical forests.
caveats: The formula only works with reflectance on a 0-1 scale: convert the values first | Mask clouds and shadows | Values far outside -1 to 1 point to scale problems or clouds

rationale: A version of NDVI that reduces the influence of bare soil. Recommended where vegetation is sparse: degraded pastures, regenerating areas, grasslands and open savannas.
caveats: The L factor (0.5 is the default) changes the result; use the same L for all images | Requires reflectance on a 0-1 scale | Mask clouds and shadows

rationale: The red edge is a spectral region very sensitive to chlorophyll. NDRE detects differences in vegetation vigor and stress even where NDVI has already saturated.
caveats: Only available on sensors with red-edge bands (e.g. Sentinel-2 B5 to B7), not on Landsat | On Sentinel-2 these bands are 20 m: resample them to match the 10 m bands | Mask clouds and shadows

rationale: Shortwave infrared is absorbed by the water inside leaves. NDMI (also known as Gao's NDWI) indicates vegetation moisture: useful for water stress, droughts and fire risk.
caveats: Resample SWIR when its resolution differs from NIR | Compare dates from the same season | Mask clouds and shadows

rationale: Water reflects green light and absorbs almost all near infrared. NDWI highlights rivers, lakes and flooded areas; positive values usually indicate water.
caveats: Built-up areas and bare soil can also have high values; MNDWI separates them better | The water/non-water threshold (e.g. 0) varies between scenes: check it on the image | Sediment-laden rivers (such as the Jurua) reflect more and may get lower values

rationale: Replaces near infrared with shortwave infrared, which water absorbs even more. It separates water from built-up areas better and is useful for mapping floodplains and wetlands.
caveats: On Sentinel-2, SWIR is 20 m and green is 10 m: resample first | Choose the water threshold by looking at the image | Terrain and cloud shadows may look like water

rationale: Burned areas lose near-infrared reflectance and gain shortwave-infrared reflectance. NBR highlights burn scars; the difference between before and after the fire (dNBR) indicates burn severity.
caveats: For dNBR, use pre- and post-fire images from the same season | Smoke and clouds get in the way: apply a mask | Recently cleared areas may also have low NBR

analysis: Supervised land use and land cover classification
rationale: With several bands, each cover type (forest, pasture, water, urban) has its own spectral signature. You provide examples of each class and an algorithm (e.g. Random Forest) classifies the rest of the image.
caveats: Requires labeled training samples (points or polygons for each class) | Validate with independent samples (confusion matrix, accuracy) | Mask clouds and use images from the same date or season

analysis: Supervised classification with your own samples
rationale: Your points or polygons have a column with classes (e.g. forest, pasture, water) and fall on the image: they can serve as training samples to classify the whole image and to measure the map's accuracy.
caveats: Check that the classes in the column are the ones you want to map and that each has enough samples (dozens per class) | Keep part of the samples for validation; do not assess the map with the training samples | Samples should be from the same period as the image

rationale: The algorithm (e.g. k-means) groups similar pixels without training samples. It is a good first exploration of the landscape.
caveats: Clusters have no names: you interpret what each one represents | The number of clusters is your choice; try a few values | Clouds and shadows form their own clusters

rationale: Comparing images of the same area on different dates (e.g. NDVI difference) shows where deforestation, regrowth, floods or river channel changes happened.
caveats: Use the same sensor, the same value scale and, if possible, the same season | Images must be aligned (same grid and CRS) | Different clouds and shadows between dates create false changes

rationale: With many dates you can test, pixel by pixel, whether an index (e.g. NDVI) is increasing or decreasing over time.
caveats: Separate seasonality (natural variation within the year) from the trend | Nearby dates and neighboring pixels are not independent observations | Cloud gaps reduce the number of observations per pixel

rationale: Slope measures how steep the terrain is. It influences erosion, runoff, species distribution and land use.
caveats: Check that elevation is in meters | In very flat areas (such as most of the Jurua floodplain), small DEM errors become false slopes | Radar DEMs (SRTM, Copernicus) measure the canopy top in forests, not the ground

rationale: Shows which direction each slope faces (north, south, east, west). It affects sunlight and soil moisture and therefore vegetation.
caveats: Aspect is meaningless on flat areas | Check that elevation is in meters | Near the equator the effect of aspect on sunlight is smaller

rationale: From the DEM you compute where water flows (flow direction) and how much area drains to each point (flow accumulation). These give the drainage network and watershed boundaries.
caveats: Fill spurious DEM depressions first | In very flat floodplains the result is sensitive to DEM errors and to the forest canopy | The accumulation threshold that defines a stream is your choice

analysis: Extraction of raster values at points
rationale: Brings the raster values at each location into the points table (e.g. NDVI, elevation). It is the bridge between field data (plots, species occurrences) and remote sensing.
caveats: Raster and points must be in the same CRS | Compare the pixel size with the GPS error; consider averaging within a radius (buffer) | Points over clouds or NA get no value

rationale: Summarizes the raster values inside each polygon (mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum), for example the mean NDVI of each plot, property or protected area.
caveats: Raster and polygons must be in the same CRS | Edge pixels fall only partly inside the polygon; for small polygons, weight by area (exactextractr package) | Polygons smaller than a pixel may get no value

rationale: The raster looks like a class map (e.g. MapBiomas), where each number is a cover type. With it you can measure landscape composition and configuration: percentage of each class, number and size of patches, amount of edge. These metrics are widely used in fragmentation and connectivity studies.
caveats: Use a projected CRS (meters); in degrees the areas are wrong | Check the legend to know what each number means | Results depend on resolution and extent (scale): compare landscapes with the same extent and resolution | Patches cut by the crop edge look smaller than they are
